samples.question: The page shows exactly four thin dark arcs: one near the top edge, one near the bottom edge, one near the left edge and one near the right edge. Every pale grey blob is background clutter and must be ignored. All four arcs are drawn in the same dark colour with the same thickness, the same length and the same curvature, so colour, thickness, length, curvature and the amount of ink say nothing about the answer. Because the four arcs share one curvature, each arc is a piece of a circle of one common size, and the only thing that tells those circles apart is where the centre of each circle lies. Exactly two of the four arcs are pieces of one and the same circle, that is, the two arcs whose circles have the same centre; each of the other two arcs belongs to a circle with a different centre. Continue each arc into its whole circle and report which two arcs share a circle, naming each of the two by the page edge it lies near. No single arc can settle this: only the agreement between two of them can. Answer unclear if no two arcs share a circle, or if two different pairs of arcs come so close to sharing a circle that the sharing pair cannot be told apart. Which two arcs lie on the same circle: top and bottom, left and right, top and left, top and right, bottom and left, bottom and right, or unclear?
